rationale: The book's case correctly separates lamp oil (Ex 25:6; 27:20 pure beaten olive for light) from anointing oil and shows that common Spirit-as-oil equations rest on the wrong substance; it also rightly notes that the Spirit is a gift that cannot be bought or measured out (Acts 8:18-20; John 3:34), so the parable's zero-sum refusal and 'buy for yourselves' language (Matt 25:8-9) sit awkwardly with a pure Spirit reading. Proverbs 21:20, 23:23 and 27:5-9, Psalm 141:5, and the fool/wise contrast of Matt 7:24-27 further support that oil is something stored by hearing-and-doing. Yet the positive identification—oil = 'Spirit-taught truth and correction received, kept, and worked into proven obedience'—is still a composite construction rather than a direct scriptural definition. No text states 'oil is the fruit of the Spirit' or 'oil is bought truth'; Zech 4:6-14 never equates the oil with the Spirit (or with obedience), and Ezek 36:27 places the Spirit as the cause of walking, not the oil itself. The chain therefore requires an extra interpretive step that collapses fruit, obedience, and stored works into the oil while still invoking the Spirit as producer. That leaves the strongest counter-readings—readiness/watchfulness without further allegory (the parable's own conclusion, Matt 25:13) and good works/charity that keep the lamp of profession burning (Matt 5:16 + following judgment scene)—still viable and textually closer. The sources therefore under-carry the book's precise central claim.
decisive_sources: Exodus 25:6; 27:20 (lamp oil distinct from anointing oil)
Proverbs 21:20; 23:23; 27:5-9; Psalm 141:5 (oil with wise dwelling, buy truth, reproof as oil)
Zechariah 4:6-14; Ezekiel 36:27 (Spirit as power/cause, never identified as the oil)
Acts 8:18-20; John 3:34 (Spirit not purchasable or finite)
unresolved_objections: No single text defines lamp oil as 'Spirit-taught truth worked into proven obedience'; the identification remains a multi-step inference.
Matthew 25:13 and the readiness discourse (24:42-44) still favor a non-allegorical reading of preparedness over any specific oil referent.
Matthew 5:16 plus the immediately following deeds-of-mercy judgment (25:31-46) keep the patristic 'good works/charity' reading competitive.
Even after distinguishing lamp oil from anointing oil, the book still leans on Spirit texts (Ezek 36:27; Zech 4; Gal 5:22) without a direct equation of oil to fruit/obedience.
